# Australia’s first Children’s Comprehensive Cancer Centre opens to deliver world leading cancer care

In an Australian first, children and young people with cancer, and their families, will benefit from world leading, comprehensive, research led clinical care in one fully integrated, purpose-built facility.
  * The Hon Mark Butler MP
Minister for Health and Ageing
Minister for Disability and the National Disability Insurance Scheme

Media event date:

6 May 2026

Date published:

6 May 2026

Media type:

Media release

In an Australian first, children and young people with cancer, and their families, will benefit from world leading, comprehensive, research led clinical care in one fully integrated, purpose-built facility.

The Minderoo Children’s Comprehensive Cancer Centre (MCCCC) unites leading researchers, clinicians and educators from Children’s Cancer Institute, Sydney Children’s Hospitals Network and UNSW Sydney – ushering in a new era of bedside-to-bench-to-bedside treatment.

The Centre was completed as part of the $658 million Sydney Children’s Hospital Stage One and Minderoo Children’s Comprehensive Cancer Centre project and was officially opened today by Federal Health Minister Mark Butler, NSW Parliamentary Secretary for Health Dr Michael Holland and Dr Andrew Forrest AO. Both the NSW and Federal Governments have financially supported the construction of the Centre with substantial philanthropic contributions from Children’s Cancer Institute, Sydney Children’s Hospital Foundation, UNSW and the Minderoo Foundation, naming rights sponsor.

The Centre spans Sydney Children’s Hospital, Randwick and adjacent UNSW Health Translation Hub, where researchers, clinicians and educators work collaboratively to accelerate treatment discoveries from labs to nearby hospital beds of cancer patients. 

The MCCCC includes: 

  * State-of-the-art research laboratories
  * Modern, family centred oncology inpatient units
  * A new day oncology treatment space
  * Dedicated education, training and research facilities
  * Shared spaces designed to foster staff connection and collaboration

Families will benefit from light-filled, private inpatient bedrooms equipped with an ensuite and carer bed, more play and recreational spaces, a kitchen to prepare meals, an outdoor terrace and a laundry.

## Latest updates

### October 2026

Resource consent has been granted by Nelson City Council for the new 128-bed inpatient unit. Phil Wheble, Group Director of Operations for Nelson Marlborough, says securing resource consent reflects the significant planning and collaboration that has gone into preparing for the new Inpatient Unit and provides certainty as the project moves into the next phase of delivery.

The new inpatient unit will deliver at least 41 additional adult medical and surgical beds and support new models of care. It will include an acute assessment unit, a patient transit lounge, a pharmacy, and assessment, treatment, and rehabilitation services, along with essential back-of-house functions.

### September 2026

Health Minister Simeon Brown visited Nelson Hospital to turn the sod to mark the beginning of early works for the new 128-bed inpatient unit. Early works are an important first step in preparing the site for construction of the new inpatient unit and will take around 12 months. This work includes service diversions, earthworks, piling, and ground improvement works.

The seven modules that form the 28-bed interim inpatient unit have now been craned into place onsite. Over the coming months, work will focus on weatherproofing, connecting services, completing the internal fit-out, and commissioning the new ward ready to welcome patients.

### July 2026

Nelson Hospital oncology services has relocated from Levels 4 and 5 of the Percy Brunette building to 34 Franklyn Street, next to the dialysis unit. This relocation is part of wider changes taking place across the campus in preparation for the construction of the new inpatient unit later this year.

### May 2026

Procurement is underway for the main contractor to deliver the multi-storey carpark building. 
If you are visiting Nelson Hospital:

  * where possible, please enter the campus via Tipahi Street and park in the main public carpark (A).
  * if parking in the Dalton carpark (C) and you need to access the main entrance, please walk out to Franklyn Street and follow the pedestrian footpath.
  * Car parking remains available via Franklyn Street for those accessing the emergency department or the medical and injury centre.

The shuttle buggy service provides free, all-weather transport for patients and visitors between the main entrance, oncology and dialysis units, and the emergency department, via all carparks. Operated by The Shuttle Buggy Trust through donations, the service operates between 8.30am to 4.30pm.

Users can access the service via the marked call points on the map below, or by contacting main reception on 03 546 1800.

Nelson Hospital campus map

These documents outline Cabinet decisions on the Programme Business Case for the Nelson Hospital redevelopment – Project Whakatupuranga.

Cabinet approved Option One of the Programme Business Case at an estimated cost of $1.098 billion, commencement of the design and enabling works for Phase One, and the Detailed Business Case (DBC) for Phase Two.

The Detailed Business Case for Phase Two was approved in April 2025.

Minderoo Children's Comprehensive Cancer Centre

The NSW and Federal Governments have partnered with the Children’s Cancer Institute, Sydney Children’s Hospitals Network (including the Kids Cancer Centre), and UNSW Sydney to create Australia’s first Children’s Comprehensive Cancer Centre.

For almost 40 years, the Children’s Cancer Institute and Kids Cancer Centre have worked together to turn scientific discoveries into real treatments for children at Sydney Children’s Hospital, Randwick.

By bringing scientists, clinicians, and educators together in one place, the new centre will speed up cancer research and improve treatments for kids.

The centre includes:

  * state-of-the-art wet and dry laboratory spaces
  * spaces for education, training, and research
  * comfortable retreat areas for patients and families
  * new oncology inpatient units
  * a new day oncology unit.


The new Prince of Wales Hospital ASB includes:

  * an expanded adult Emergency Department
  * an expanded Intensive Care Unit
  * a new digital operating theatres equipped with state-of-the-art technology
  * a new shared medical imaging department
  * a new and expanded Central Sterilizing Services Department
  * a new helipad servicing the Randwick Hospitals Campus (operational from early 2026)
  * an expanded Psychiatric Emergency Care Centre
  * a new Community Assessment Unit
  * Community Management Centre
  * Replacement of existing inpatient wards and provision of additional inpatient beds providing contemporary facilities for the following specialties:
    * haematology and oncology
    * aged care (acute and rehabilitation)
    * orthopaedics
    * general surgery and specialty surgery
    * respiratory and infectious diseases
    * clinical neurosciences floor that will incorporate an expanded Acute Stroke Unit, neurology and neurosurgical beds and the Complex Epilepsy Service
    * research, education and training spaces, including additional spaces funded by UNSW Sydney, to enable clinical innovation and research, biomedical engineering, and clinical translational research laboratories co-located directly alongside clinical staff providing acute healthcare services.

The ASB is the first major upgrade to the Prince of Wales Hospital in 25 years, delivering state-of-the-art infrastructure that will support new and innovative approaches to acute healthcare and provide staff with purpose-designed and built facilities that support contemporary clinical practice.

Health-related academic and translational research spaces will be co-located with clinical services. These include laboratories and spaces to support collaboration and the testing and trialing of new models of care and innovative treatments.

# Internal Medicine Specialist | Wellington, NZ

 

A New Hospital. A New Chapter. Internal Medicine Specialist, ARC Wellington

 

Imagine helping establish an internal medicine service in a new specialist and emergency hospital.

Imagine having the clinical challenge of complex referral medicine, colleagues who value collaboration, and the chance to help shape how a service works from its first day.

Now imagine finishing work in a city where the waterfront, native bush and a good café are all close by.

ARC Vets is opening a purpose-built emergency and specialty hospital in Wellington in late 2027. We’re looking for a Small Animal Internal Medicine Specialist to join us in late 2027 or early 2028.

Why Join ARC Wellington?

Joining a new hospital is a chance to help establish its clinical culture, referral relationships and ways of working from the outset.

We envisage a two-specialist internal medicine service as ARC Wellington develops. Our aim is to build a service where internists can share cases, exchange ideas and support one another, while each has the opportunity to help shape its direction.

You’ll also be part of ARC’s wider specialist community. Our Auckland hospitals are home to four registered internal medicine specialists, as well as colleagues in diagnostic imaging, oncology, neurology, emergency and critical care, surgery and ophthalmology. You’ll be able to draw on that network for discussion, shared learning and collaboration as you establish the Wellington service.

Locally, you’ll work alongside colleagues in emergency medicine, surgery and other developing services. You’ll have the opportunity to help create the close, practical collaboration that makes a multidisciplinary hospital work well for patients.

At ARC, we want referring veterinarians to feel confident involving us in their patients’ care. That means being approachable, communicating clearly and making it easy to work together. It also means treating clients with kindness and giving patients the thoughtful, high-quality care they deserve.

About the Role

You’ll provide specialist internal medicine services within a multidisciplinary referral hospital. 
You bring sound clinical judgement, curiosity and a willingness to ask for another perspective when it will help a patient. You enjoy working across disciplines and building relationships with referring vets. You communicate with care, including when cases are complicated or decisions are difficult.

Why ARC?

ARC Vets is an independent, veterinarian-owned New Zealand emergency and specialty hospital group, with two established hospitals in Auckland and our third opening in Wellington.

Our values guide how we work: we are one team, we do right by our patients, we value growth, we take ownership and we make referrals easy. We believe excellent specialist medicine depends on skilled people who share their knowledge and support one another.

At Wellington, you’ll have the opportunity to help build a new service, with an established network of specialists to learn from and collaborate with.

 

Why Wellington?

An international move is a big decision. The role needs to be right, and so does the life around it.

Wellington is a compact, creative city with a strong food and arts scene, a beautiful harbour and easy access to walking tracks, beaches and the outdoors. For specialists looking for a change of pace without giving up challenging clinical work, it has a great deal to offer.

We welcome applications from New Zealand and overseas. If you’re interested but still working out the timing and practicalities of a move, we’d be pleased to start a conversation.

What’s Next?

If you’d like to practice excellent internal medicine and help establish a service you’re proud of, we’d love to hear from you.

Apply now with your CV though our website and tell us what interests you about ARC Wellington. As we can't fit everything into a job advertisement, if you have questions about the role, get in touch by email to fiona.park@arcvets.co.nz

# Life-changing cancer care closer to home in Northland

  * Hon Simeon Brown

Health

Construction of the new radiation oncology service at Whangārei Hospital is now complete, bringing cancer treatment closer to home for Northlanders, Health Minister Simeon Brown says.

"This is a significant milestone for Northland and a major step forward for cancer care in the region,” Mr Brown says.

"Right now, many Northlanders face lengthy journeys to Auckland for radiation treatment, with return journeys ranging from 320 to 620 kilometres between Whangārei and Kaitaia. Cancer treatment is challenging enough without the added burden of spending hours on the road, away from family and the comforts of home.

“Once the service opens, most patients will be able to receive treatment in Whangārei, reducing travel and allowing them to spend more time with their families and support networks."

Currently, around 450 people travel to Auckland annually for radiation treatment.

Pepe Reading, left and Rian McGann, Registered Nurses – Oncology, and Shelley Shea, Charge Nurse Manager and Head of Department for Oncology, are welcoming patients into the new facility. Photo: Supplied.

Cancer patients and their whānau are being welcomed into a new oncology facility at the Nelson Hospital campus, bringing chemotherapy treatment and outpatient cancer clinics together under one roof for the first time.

Located alongside the dialysis unit on Franklyn Street, the refurbished facility replaces services previously delivered across two separate locations on the hospital campus.

The move increases treatment capacity, with an additional treatment space allowing seven patients to receive infusions at the same time. Larger clinical areas also meet national healthcare standards and are designed to support growing demand for cancer services across the Nelson Marlborough region.

# Australia’s first Wildlife Specialist Teaching Hospital at Taronga

Published:
    16 April 2025
Released by:
    The Premier, Minister for Environment and Heritage

Listen

* * *

Construction has now started on Australia’s first ever wildlife specialist teaching veterinary hospital, at Taronga Zoo in Sydney.

This $80 million state-of-the-art facility will replace the current hospital, which has played a critical role in wildlife care since the 1970’s.

The new Taronga Wildlife Hospital will expand the zoo’s critical rescue and rehabilitation work by delivering new surgical, rehabilitation and recovery facilities to cater for hundreds of animals per year.

As a dedicated specialist teaching hospital, it will also enable widespread training and upskilling of wildlife carers, students and veterinary practitioners – further protecting Australia’s unique biodiversity against ever increasing natural disasters.

The 2019-2020 Black Summer bushfires affected billions of animals, including koalas, wallabies, platypus and critically endangered amphibians which Taronga’s hospital team was instrumental in treating.
